content: A superficial vein refers to a vein that is located close to the surface of the body. This term is used to distinguish these veins from deep veins, which are situated further away from the surface. Unlike deep veins, superficial veins are not accompanied by an artery of the same name running alongside them. In contrast, deep veins are typically paired with arteries that share the same name. Superficial veins play a significant physiological role in thermoregulation. When the body becomes overheated, blood is redirected from the deep veins to the superficial veins to facilitate heat dissipation to the surrounding environment. These veins are often visible beneath the skin, and those located below the level of the heart tend to bulge outward. A simple way to observe this phenomenon is by raising your hand above your heart, which causes the blood to drain from the veins, or lowering it below your heart, which causes the veins to fill with blood. Superficial veins become more prominent visually during activities such as lifting heavy weights, particularly after consistent strength training. However, from a physiological perspective, superficial veins are less critical than deep veins because they carry a smaller volume of blood. For this reason, superficial veins are sometimes surgically removed in a procedure called vein stripping, which is commonly performed to treat varicose veins. Some named superficial veins include the external jugular vein. In the upper limb, examples of superficial veins are the cephalic vein and the median cubital vein. The median cubital vein is frequently used for venipuncture, the process of drawing blood.
